info.bio:
Grupo canadiense, formado a principios de los años 60, en sus comienzos usaron el nombre de "The Hawks", ya que fueron el grupo de acompañamiento del rockero Ronnie Hawkins, conocido como "the Hawk" (El Halcón).

Sus miembros eran:

Robbie Robertson (1942) guitarrista
Levon Helm (1941-2012) bateria y voz
Rick Danko (1942-1999) bajo y voz
Richard Manuel (1943-1986) Teclados y voz
Garth Hudson (1940) multinstrumentista

Empezaron a hacerse un nombre tras la electrificación de Bob Dylan

scenes.desc: En los setenta, el reajuste a los viejos valores (blues, folk, country) convierte al rock en uno de los mayores éxitos del consumismo: el Establishment ya no intenta destruirlo, lo absorbe. El country-rock de Gram Parsons es una moda enorme: Commander Cody, New Riders Of The Purple Sage, Manassas, Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Poco y los Eagles (Desperado, Hotel California); en Nashville surgen los «outlaws» (Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson). El roots-rock sigue con Hot Tuna, Little Feat y Doobie Brothers, y la nostalgia recupera el blues (Roy Buchanan, Bonnie Raitt), la armonía vocal (Manhattan Transfer, Roches, McGarrigle Sisters) y los cincuenta (American Graffiti).

podcast.body: Robbie Robertson was the guitarist, musical director, and chief songwriter of the Band — a Canadian group widely credited with helping create the genre of Americana. "It's interesting how a Canadian band helped create a whole new genre of music called Americana."

xref.title: Band Name Origin (1963)
xref.body: While rehearsing in Birmingham, England, across from a cinema playing a 1963 horror movie titled "Black Sabbath," bassist Geezer Butler observed people paying good money to be scared. This sparked the idea for the band to create music that would also scare and shock people, leading them to rename themselves from "Earth" to "Black Sabbath" after the movie. "One day they noticed that the cinema was playing a 1963 horror movie entitled Black Sabbath."

xref.title: Disastrous Merchandising Deal (1963)
xref.body: In 1963, Beatles manager Brian Epstein licensed the band's merchandising rights to Nikki Bern's company, Selltab (Beatles spelled backwards). This deal secured only 10% of revenues for The Beatles and is estimated to have cost the band over $100 million over the years, despite selling a wide array of items from wigs to bubblegum. "In retrospect, this was a stupid deal, securing just 10% in revenues for the band."

xref.title: Brief Montreal Stay (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles played two concerts at the Montreal Forum on September 8, 1964, performing a 12-song set for 9,500 fans at 5:20 pm and another show for 11,500 fans at 8:30 pm. They chose not to stay in Montreal, instead flying directly to Jacksonville, Florida, having been in the city for only eight hours. "The band stayed in Montreal for only 8 hours."

xref.title: Brief Vancouver Performance (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' concert in Vancouver on August 22, 1964, despite the massive anticipation and crowd frenzy, lasted only 27 minutes. They played 11 songs, notably omitting "I Want to Hold Your Hand," one of their biggest hits at the time. Immediately after the show, the band was whisked away to Vancouver International Airport and flown straight to Los Angeles, marking their one and only performance in Western Canada. "Then just 27 minutes after they arrived on stage, they left."

xref.title: Bryce Decker's Airport Escapade (1964)
xref.body: On August 18, 1964, local high school student Bryce Decker took a daring chance at Winnipeg airport during The Beatles' refueling stop. He ran across the runway, climbed the plane's stairs, and nearly entered the aircraft before being restrained by security, an escapade that was captured in a series of photographs. Decker later recalled seeing the band members chuckling as security wrestled with him, having "just did it for a bit of fun" without realizing its significance. "After arriving at the airport, he ran across the runway, up the stairs, and nearly got into the plane before he was grouted by security."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Concert Logistics at Maple Leaf Gardens (1964)
xref.body: For the September 6, 1964, concerts at Maple Leaf Gardens, a detailed plan was devised to get The Beatles safely to the venue. Limousines served as a decoy, drawing fans while the band slipped out the back door of the King Edward Hotel and into a paddy wagon, which smuggled them into the Gardens. A five-block area around the venue was sectioned off 12 hours prior, transforming downtown Toronto into "Beedleland." "Limos were to pull up at the King Edward Hotel, as expected, as fans pounded at the vehicles like zombies the band would dug out the back door and into a patty wagon that would smuggle them into the gardens."

xref.title: First North American Tour Stop in Winnipeg (1964)
xref.body: On a warm, cloudy day in mid-August 1964, The Beatles were flying from London to San Francisco for their inaugural major North American tour, making an unplanned refueling stop in Winnipeg. This stop unexpectedly turned into a major event when CJAYTV's Bob Burns announced their arrival on local radio, leading to the airport being swarmed by frenzied fans. "The band landed on August 18, 1964 at 2.5pm."

xref.title: Hotel Invasion by Fans (1964)
xref.body: During The Beatles' stay at the King Edward Hotel in Toronto in September 1964, teens relentlessly bypassed security, creating an "infestation" for which the hotel seemed to have "no repellent." At 3 am, radio journalist Larry Cain, traveling with the band, encountered a teen in an oversized housekeeping uniform knocking on his door, asking for soap and then if he could take her to The Beatles. "Teens kept getting past security. It was as if the hotel was dealing with an infestation for which they had no repellent."

xref.title: Intentional Speaker Damage for Distortion (1964)
xref.body: Dave Davies was an early pioneer in physically modifying amplifiers to achieve distortion. In 1964, while recording a song with The Kinks, he intentionally damaged the speaker cone of his small amplifier, using either a razor blade or a screwdriver, to produce a distorted sound. While effective in creating the desired effect, this method offered little control over the specific type or intensity of the distortion. "When the band was recording this song in 1964, he slashed the speaker cone of his small amp."

xref.title: John Lennon's Clash with Red Robinson (1964)
xref.body: Halfway through the Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, as the crowd neared rioting, local radio host Red Robinson was instructed to go on stage to calm the fans. John Lennon, unaware of the situation, confronted Robinson, telling him, "Get off our stage, nobody interrupts the Beatles," before relenting after Robinson explained that manager Brian Epstein had sent him. "John looked down at Brian Epstein, the band's manager who gave him the okay. John turned Robinson and said, Okay, carry on mate."

xref.title: King Edward Hotel Frenzy (1964)
xref.body: Upon their arrival at the King Edward Hotel in downtown Toronto on September 6, 1964, a frenzy of fans greeted The Beatles, leading to Paul McCartney having his shirt torn and Ringo Starr being separated from John and George. Although police quickly restored order on the street, Beatlemania continued inside, where a 14-year-old girl was found hiding in the linen closet of their royal suite. "Paul would have a shirt torn open by a fan, wrangle with separated from John and George, but thankfully police were able to quickly restore order on the street and get the band into the hotel."

xref.title: Mass Hysteria at Maple Leaf Gardens (1964)
xref.body: Upon The Beatles' appearance on stage at Maple Leaf Gardens on September 6, 1964, flash bulbs went off, blinding everyone, and the roar of 16,761 screaming voices made it impossible to hear the music, blinding and deafening the band. Items like bras and lipsticks rained down, leading to 109 fans fainting at the venue, described as "mass hysteria" rather than just a rock show. "It's unclear if they could even hear their own voices over the roar of 16,761 streaming voices, nor do we know if they could see anything as bras, lipsticks, and other items rain down on them."

xref.title: Massive Police Deployment in Toronto (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' first visit to Toronto in September 1964 necessitated an extraordinary police response, with more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario Provincial Police, and the counties called in. By noon, 4,000 police officers and auxiliaries were on duty around Maple Leaf Gardens, dividing the crowd into smaller sections, with majestic horses used to push back waves of "deranged youth." "The band's first visit to Toronto required more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario provincial police, and the counties."

xref.title: Minimal Commercial Success (1964-1973)
xref.body: During their nine years together, The Velvet Underground achieved "pretty much zero commercial success," selling very few records, playing sparsely attended gigs, and almost never getting airplay on underground FM radio, indicating their profound disconnect from the mainstream music industry of the time. "But in the nine years the band was together, the velvet underground had pretty much zero commercial success. They sold very few records. Their gigs were sparsely attended. And even in the era of underground FM radio almost no one played their records."

xref.title: Pan Am Flight 101 Arrival - February 7, 1964
xref.body: The band's arrival on Pan Am Flight 101 from London at JFK Airport in New York on February 7, 1964, symbolized a massive explosion of Britishness and national pride. This event was referenced as a benchmark for the level of national pride seen again during the Britpop era. "an explosion of pride in Britishness that we really hadn't seen since February 7, 1964 when Pan Am Flight 101 from London touched down at JFK Airport in New York carrying a band called The Beatles."

xref.title: Paul McCartney Greets Winnipeg (1964)
xref.body: Following the incident with Bryce Decker at the Winnipeg airport on August 18, 1964, Paul McCartney exited the plane, yelled "Hello, Winnipeg," and descended the stairs, where he was immediately swarmed by a throng of reporters, including Bob Burns. This brief appearance was the band's only direct interaction with the Winnipeg crowd, as they never returned to the city. "Oh, and the man who greeted the crowd was none other than Paul McCartney."

xref.title: Peaceful Departure from Toronto (1964)
xref.body: The day after their chaotic concerts, just before noon on September 7, 1964, The Beatles headed back to the Toronto airport. The sun was shining, the crowd was considerably smaller than the previous day, and the mood was distinctly different. The band signed autographs, posed for photos, waved to their admirers, and then boarded their plane, marking the end of their first Toronto visit. "The sun was shining, and the crowd was considerably smaller. The mood was also different. This was the end."

xref.title: Vancouver Concert Delay and Paperwork (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, was scheduled for 8 pm, but a significant delay occurred because the pilot of their plane forgot to sign a required document. This forced the band to return to the airport to complete the paperwork, while 20,000 fans impatiently waited at the stadium. "The show was supposed to start at 8pm, but the pilot of the plane bringing the Beatles to Canada forgot to sign a document, and the band was forced to return to the airport to finish the paperwork and then head back to the stadium."

xref.title: Appearance in 1965
xref.body: The band first appeared in 1965 during a time when rock and roll was considered disposable, AM radio-oriented, and not "serious music." Their arrival signaled a shift towards deeper, more sophisticated, and existential music that demanded respect. "When they first appeared in 1965, rock and roll, which is what we call the singles oriented music about basically cars and girls and that sort of thing, was still largely considered to be disposable, effervescent."

xref.title: Discovery and Patronage by Andy Warhol (December 1965)
xref.body: One night, just as The Velvet Underground faced a second firing from Cafe Bizarre, Andy Warhol and his entourage, including groupies and "weirdos," unexpectedly visited the club. Warhol was so profoundly impressed by their "avant-garde approach to rock" that he immediately signed them to be his official house band at his performance art headquarters, The Factory, located on East 47th Street. Warhol assumed the roles of their patron, producer, and promoter, a pivotal moment that launched the band's "long, strange road to becoming legends as the first alternative rock band in history." "Andy Warhol adopts the Velvet Underground, thereby giving the band the break they needed, to eventually be hailed as the founders of alternative rock"

xref.title: Return to Toronto and Fading Beatlemania (1965)
xref.body: On August 17, 1965, The Beatles returned to Canada, flying in from New York to Pearson Airport (then Toronto International Airport), where fans again rushed them, met by Toronto police. They stayed at the King Edward Hotel, where "smart fans" booked dozens of rooms. However, the enthusiasm had waned slightly, as newspaper coverage shifted from front-page headlines to inside pages, with many suggesting that Beatlemania was fading and the band's popularity might soon disappear. "Unlike the previous year when the band made front page news in Toronto, this year, they were on the inside pages, with many starting to say that Biddlemania was fading, and the band would soon disappear."

xref.title: Shea Stadium Sound Disaster (1965)
xref.body: When The Beatles played Shea Stadium on August 15, 1965, there was no proper concert sound system for the venue. They set up on a small stage, using a bunch of mics and a couple of 100 Watt Vox amplifiers, and pumped everything through the stadium's public address system—the same speakers and amplifiers used for baseball announcements. It was so bad that the Beatles not only couldn't be heard by the audience but also couldn't hear themselves. "As a last second fix, one of the road crew flipped over some of their amplifiers and pointed them directly at the band."

xref.title: Troubled Residency at Cafe Bizarre (December 1965)
xref.body: In December 1965, this "new and very weird group" secured their first regular gig at Cafe Bizarre in Greenwich Village, New York City. They were commissioned to perform six sets nightly, six nights a week, for five dollars per set. However, their avant-garde music often had the unintended effect of chasing away patrons rather than attracting them, leading to the band being fired at least once for driving customers away. "the band's music ten to do chase away patrons instead of luring them in and the band was fired at least once for driving away customers."

xref.title: Early Lo-Fi Aesthetic (1966-1967)
xref.body: The band, composed of broke musicians associated with Andy Warhol, aimed to make a record with a meager budget of possibly $1,500. Their debut album, released in March 1967, was characterized by significant hiss, distortion, recording errors, a rough final mix, and poor stereo imaging, with singer Nico often being off-key. Despite these technical flaws, the primitive sound contributed to its appeal for a segment of music fans who valued authenticity and rebellion. "The Velvet Underground's records were generally derided for sounding bad, which made all kind of sense in the late 1960s and the early 1970s because the goal back then was to achieve perfect sound or something close to it."

xref.title: Last Canadian and Touring Concerts (1966)
xref.body: The Beatles returned to Canada on August 17, 1966, for their final two concerts ever on Canadian soil in Toronto. This tour also marked the last time the band would ever play live, consisting of only eight shows over 12 days before they stopped touring forever to focus exclusively on studio music. "Just a year later in 1966, the band returned for their last two concerts ever on Canadian soil. The tour was also the last the band would ever play."

xref.title: Scepter Studios Demos (1966) – Discovered by Warren Hill
xref.body: On April 25, 1966, The Velvet Underground recorded demos at Scepter Studios in New York, resulting in two acetate test pressings that were circulated to record companies, all of whom declined to sign the band. The band later signed with Verve, re-recording their material. In 2002, Warren Hill found one of these acetates at a flea market in Chelsea, New York, for 75 cents. After researching its rarity, he auctioned it on eBay for $25,200, and it has since been digitized for wider listening. "What he had bought was one of only two copies of this test pressing. xref.title: Debut Performance at CBGB (August 14, 1974)
xref.body: On Wednesday, August 14, 1974, The Ramones played their first-ever show at the iconic New York club CBGB. The initial audience was sparse, consisting of fewer than a dozen people, including the club owner's dog. However, by the end of 1974, the band had performed at CBGB 74 times, with each gig progressively increasing their buzz. The club soon became packed with a diverse crowd, attracting Andy Warhol's circle, intellectuals, wealthy uptown youths seeking to "slum it," and music fans bored with existing sounds and looking for novelty. The Ramones' distinctive style — four "brothers" dressed in torn jeans and leather jackets, playing 1960s-style "bubble gum pop songs" at "a million miles an hour," without solos, stage interaction, or audience acknowledgment, pausing only when Johnny counted off the next song — marked the genesis of the New York punk rock revolution. "The Ramones played their first ever show at a New York club called CBGB."

xref.title: First Show October 17, 1975 – Pre-dates Sex Pistols and The Clash; 1980 Ontario Place Riot
xref.body: Teenage Head formed in Hamilton, Ontario, and played their first show on October 17, 1975 at Westdale High School — three weeks before the Sex Pistols played their first gig, and nine months before The Clash formed. They were a major force in Canadian punk, combining elements of the Ramones, New York Dolls, and 1950s rock and roll. Their profile peaked with a 1980 show at Ontario Place in Toronto where thousands tried to get in; what followed became an infamous riot. American radio programmers loved the music but balked at the band name (for obvious reasons), prompting a temporary rename to "Teenage Heads" for US purposes. Just before a crucial US showcase in September 1980, guitarist Gord Lewis was in a serious car accident, canceling the shows and closing the window of opportunity. Original singer Frankie Venom died of throat cancer in 2008; the band continues with Dave Rave on vocals more than 40 years later. "Long after most of their original punk rock contemporaries called it quits, or died off, Teenage Head still with us."

xref.title: "Today" Show Interview (1976) – National Controversy
xref.body: On Wednesday, December 1st, 1976, the Sex Pistols appeared on the popular UK tea-time chat show *Today*, hosted by Bill Grundy. They were a last-minute replacement for Queen, who had to cancel due to Freddie Mercury's throat infection. The band and their entourage consumed a bottle of Blue Nun in the limo and more liquor in the green room before going on live, unaware the show was unedited. Grundy's provocative questioning led to the band using profanity on air, which resulted in Grundy's two-week suspension, the producer and director's firing, and widespread media outrage with headlines like "the filth and the fury." This 117-second incident, despite being accidental, massively boosted punk rock's profile in the UK, causing "Anarchy in the UK" sales to jump from 10,000 copies in a week to 10,000 copies a day. "The impact of that 117 second interview was immediate."

xref.body: The Ramones played two pivotal shows in London, first at the Roundhouse (capacity 2,000) on America's bicentennial, and then at Dingwalls two nights later. xref.title: Infamous "Today" TV Appearance (1976) - National Scandal

xref.title: Inspiration for British Punk (1976)
xref.body: The Ramones played a pivotal gig at the Roundhouse in London on Sunday, July 4th, 1976, as part of America's Bicentennial. Around 2,000 members of the "infant UK punk community" packed the venue, eager to hear the New York sound. This performance, along with another at Dingwalls, was immensely influential; key figures like Johnny Rotten and Joe Strummer attended soundchecks and shows, stating that the Ramones "turned them on" and "inspired them to form their own bands." The band felt like "royalty" upon arrival, noting the shift from selling out CBGB's to playing for 3,000 kids already "tuned in." "No one could have known it at the time, but this was one of the most influential gigs in the history of rock."

xref.body: Before his music career, Elvis Costello worked as a computer operator for Elizabeth Arden cosmetics, running invoices on an IBM 360 mainframe, taking occasional sick days to demo songs. An American group called Clover had just arrived in England hoping for their big break, but found themselves stranded in the middle of punk and unwanted. They needed money for plane tickets home. Elvis went to their residency at Headley Grange, told them he needed a studio band and specifically didn't need a singer, so Clover's own singer was sent to wait elsewhere while the rest of the band backed Elvis through six four-hour sessions for his debut. Clover was paid and sent back to the US, where they reinvented themselves as Huey Lewis and the News. The singer who had to hang out during the Costello sessions was Huey Lewis. xref.body: The Curse are contenders with the B-Girls for the title of Canada's first all-female punk band, having been ready to perform as early as May 1977. The following month they played CBGB in New York on a bill with the Viletones, Diodes, and Teenage Head. They were more intense than the B-Girls — member Mickey Skin performed with a fake lobotomy scar and the band had an explicitly feminist agenda, often starting food fights at shows. xref.title: Two-Tone Records Founded 1979 – Black-and-White Logo Based on Peter Tosh Photo; Anti-Racist Mission
xref.body: Jerry Dammers founded Two-Tone Records, naming it after the black-and-white suits worn by mods and skinheads of the 1960s and after the peaceful multiracial makeup of the band. The label's logo — a man in a black and white suit, white shirt, black tie, sunglasses, pork pie hat, white socks, and black loafers — was drawn by Dammers based on a photo of Peter Tosh when he was a member of the Wailers. The character was named Walt Jabsco (Walt after Walt Disney). Two-Tone had an explicit anti-racism message at a time when racial tensions in the UK were getting out of control. xref.title: Career Launch Triggered by Theft (1980)
xref.body: The band's unexpected career trajectory began when a frat boy stole a fancy and expensive Budweiser beer tap from the party, which Kathleen O'Brien had rented with a bad check deposit. xref.title: Chaotic New York Concert (May 15, 1980)
xref.body: Public Image Limited (P.I.L.), led by Johnny Lydon (formerly Johnny Rotten), agreed to play two nights at the Ritz in New York for a $12,000 fee, despite internal squabbles, drug abuse, and money problems. The band was in no shape to play, lacking a drummer (the sixth one quit) and a bass player (who had just walked out). They quickly hired a 65-year-old jazz drummer from a Broadway music shop. Instead of performing live, P.I.L. pantomimed along to their records, hidden from the audience by a large screen with their silhouettes projected by bright white lights. The 1,500 people in the audience were kept waiting in the pouring rain for over an hour, then discovered the band wasn't playing, and Johnny Lydon began taunting and insulting the crowd. This led to a rain of garbage, a storming of the stage, and the destruction of all equipment, with the gig ending after just 25 minutes. "The gig was killed after just 25 minutes."

xref.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 1980)
xref.body: Ian Curtis died by suicide on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures exacerbated by a "crazy cocktail" of prescriptions, drinking, illegal drug use, poor diet, and late nights. He also faced an impending divorce, an affair with a Belgian woman, money worries, and pressure to continue performing with Joy Division despite his problems. The final Joy Division show on May 2, 1980, saw Ian faint during the last song, experiencing another grand mal seizure, leading to the cancellation of their upcoming North American tour. On the evening of May 17, Ian returned to his home at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife Deborah was out. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank strong coffee and whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on May 18, he put on his favorite album, "The Idiot" by Iggy Pop, went to the garden for a length of rope from the clothesline, and hanged himself. Deborah found him a few hours later. "He'd been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures that were exacerbated by a crazy cocktail of prescriptions, drinking illegal drug use, poor diet late nights, an impending divorce, and a ferry was having with a woman from Belgium worries about money and pressures to keep on performing with the band despite all these problems."

xref.title: Four Lead Singers – Bon Scott Died 1980, Brian Johnson Made Back in Black, Axl Rose Subbed in 2016
xref.body: AC/DC has had four lead singers. Dave Evans was the original, present from the band's 1973 formation through their glam-rock phase. Bon Scott replaced him after being discovered working as the band's chauffeur; he recorded seven albums cementing AC/DC's reputation but died of acute alcohol poisoning on February 19, 1980. Brian Johnson replaced him in time for *Back in Black* (1980), which has sold at least 50 million copies. When Johnson developed serious ear problems in 2016, Axl Rose of Guns N' Roses sang for approximately two dozen shows; Johnson subsequently received treatment and rejoined. "The swap worked way better than anyone could have dreamed."
